# Kāma Sutta (Snp 4.1 (PTS Snp 151))

**ID:** Snp 4.1 (PTS Snp 151)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Kāma Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Sensual Pleasures
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp4.1
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāma Sutta* (Snp 4.1, PTS Snp 151, vv. 766–771) stands as the opening discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta*, directly following the *Mahāvagga* [SuttaCentral; Tournier et al.; Wayman 1997]. Early commentary recorded in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* specifies that the sixteen poems recited by Soṇa began with this discourse [Vinaya Pitaka 4]. The text examines the drawbacks and perils of sensual desire (*kāma*), warning that pursuing sense pleasures leads to affliction and suffering whenever those desires are thwarted or when the seeker is overwhelmed by cravings [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Buswell and Gimello 1992]. The term *kāma* appears six times in the poem, encompassing subjective desire, specific sense pleasures, and external sense objects [Fronsdal 2016]. Examining its metrical structure, scholars have noted that its *vatta* (śloka) verses closely adhere to classical norms, suggesting to some that it belongs to a relatively later layer than the more archaic verse strata of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* [Ruegg and Schmithausen 1990].

Within the Pali Canon and later exegetical literature, the sutta forms the subject of an entire commentary in the *Mahāniddesa* (*Kāmasuttaniddesa*, Mnd 1), which analyses *kāma* into subjective defilements (*kilesa-kāma*) and objective sense domains (*vatthu-kāma*) [SuttaCentral; Global Recovery 2010]. The verse collection is also cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 4, Ne 15), the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2), and framed in the *Jātaka* commentary as the sermon through which the Buddha consoled a grieving brahmin in the *Kāmajātaka* (Ja 467) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887].

Parallels to the sutta appear across non-Pali traditions, notably the Chinese *Arthavargīya* translation (*Yizu jing*, T 198) and the Sanskrit *Śarīrārthagāthā* preserved in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, where Asaṅga cites verses corresponding to Sn 766–770/771 as originating from the *kāmas* in the *Arthavargīya* [SuttaCentral; Lee 2017; Wayman 1997]. Resembling verses also occur in the Jain *Uttarādhyayanasūtra* 3 [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse across Mnd 1, Ne 4, Ne 15, and the *Nettivibhāvinī*, while supporting SuttaCentral's curated parallels with direct alignments to the Sanskrit *Śarīrārthagāthā* and the Tibetan translation of the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094) [DharmaNexus].

- Passage-level parallels (SuttaCentral): Sag Śarīrārthagāthā; T 198 佛說義足經; Ja 467 Kāmajātaka

- Mentioned in (SuttaCentral): Mnd 1 Kāmasuttaniddesa; Ne 15 Otaraṇahāravibhaṅga; Ne 4 Desanāhāravibhaṅga; Pe 2 Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi
